title: How Do You Stop Stakeholders From Cherry-Picking Customer Feedback Quotes?
summary: One vivid customer quote can beat a percentage in any meeting. Four rules that stop stakeholders cherry-picking feedback quotes to back their own opinion.
body_markdown:
Someone opens the roadmap meeting by reading a customer comment aloud. It's vivid, specific, and it argues for the thing they already wanted to build. The room turns. Your analysis of 4,000 comments is still on the screen and has just stopped mattering.


You can't stop people quoting customers, and you shouldn't want to. You change what a quote has to arrive with: its theme, that theme's share of feedback, and a comment from the same theme pointing the other way. Then you agree what evidence would change the decision before anyone reads a quote out loud. Thematic supports the first half directly: the Volume view shows the percentage of comments mentioning a theme, and the Comments section shows the verbatims behind it with the sentence that triggered the tag highlighted. The quote and its denominator come from the same place.


One warning first, because it's the part most advice gets wrong.[Quantifying the theme](https://getthematic.com/insights/quantify-qualitative-feedback) is necessary, but putting a percentage next to the quote isn't enough on its own. (A note on terms: in customer support, "cherry-picking" usually means agents choosing easy tickets. This is the other sense, selecting evidence for a conclusion you already hold.)


## The four rules


1. **A quote never travels without its theme and its share.** Every verbatim arrives labeled with the theme it belongs to and the percentage of feedback that theme represents.
2. **Show the quote that points the other way.** The counter-evidence has to be as vivid as the original, not a footnote under it.
3. **Agree what would change the decision before anyone reads a quote.** Set the threshold while nobody yet knows which way the evidence falls.
4. **Let people test their own theory.** Make the feedback searchable enough that a hunch can be checked before the meeting, not argued in it.


## Why the obvious fix doesn't work on its own


In 1980, Hamill, Wilson and Nisbett showed people a single vivid case and asked them to judge the whole population. Exposure to the case shifted their views whether they were told nothing about how typical it was, told it was highly typical, or[told it was highly atypical](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.39.4.578) . Saying "this is just one customer" doesn't undo the effect. The disclaimer is quiet; the story is loud.


Borgida and Nisbett had shown why. Statistical summaries lack force because of their "abstract, pallid nature," and[information is utilized in proportion to its vividness](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1559-1816.1977.tb00750.x) . A theme at 3% of feedback is pallid. A furious paragraph from a named customer is vivid. Both can sit on the same slide and the vivid one wins.


Assume good faith, because you'll usually be right. Kunda's review of motivated reasoning describes people who, wanting a particular conclusion, "attempt to be rational and to construct a justification of their desired conclusion that would persuade a dispassionate observer." The stakeholder isn't fabricating. They're reaching for the cheapest justification available, and a real customer quote is the cheapest one in the building. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes that[suppressed evidence](https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/) counts as a fallacy even when the omission is inadvertent.


So the goal isn't to catch anyone. It's to make that justification more expensive, as a standing convention rather than an accusation in the moment.


## Rule 1: A quote never travels without its theme and its share


Qualitative research settled this decades ago. The SRQR reporting standard lists findings as[one item](https://www.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/srqr/) and the evidence substantiating them as a separate one. COREQ asks whether quotations were presented "to illustrate the themes / findings" and whether each was individually identified. A quote illustrates a finding. It isn't the finding. What makes the finding hold up is being able to[trace the number back to the text](https://getthematic.com/insights/governance-controls-unified-feedback) behind it.


In practice that means a house format nobody skips, yourself included:


- The theme the quote belongs to.
- The share of feedback it represents, and over what period.
- The direction of travel: rising, flat, or falling.
- An ID, so anyone can find the original.


Thematic's Volume view gives the percentage directly, and hovering a theme in the Comparison tool gives the exact count. One counting rule matters: base theme volume counts each tagged response once, so sub-theme volumes don't necessarily sum to the base total. No feature stamps a share-of-feedback badge onto a quote, so this is a discipline you apply, not a setting you switch on.


Volume alone isn't the whole answer. A theme mentioned often may move your score less than a smaller one, which is why Impact Analysis compares the score across all responses with the score excluding that theme. Where the argument is about what to fix first,[rank by impact rather than volume](https://getthematic.com/insights/prioritize-product-roadmap-customer-feedback) .


## Rule 2: Show the quote that points the other way


Telling a room to be objective doesn't work well. Lord, Lepper and Preston found that prompting people to[consider the opposite](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.47.6.1231) had a greater corrective effect than instructions to be as fair and unbiased as possible.


The practical version is a slide convention, and it sits inside whatever structure you already use for[reporting findings to executives](https://getthematic.com/insights/report-customer-feedback-findings-executive-team) . Any theme worth a quote gets two: the strongest comment for and the strongest against, from the same theme and period. In Thematic the Comments section under a theme is color-coded by sentiment, so finding the opposing verbatim takes seconds.


This makes the counter-evidence as vivid as the original, which is the only thing the research says reliably competes with a vivid case. It also changes the dynamic: the person who brought the quote isn't being contradicted by a percentage, they're being shown another customer.


## Rule 3: Agree what would change the decision before anyone reads a quote


This is the move almost nobody makes, and the one that settles arguments. It assumes you have agreed[one authoritative feedback layer](https://getthematic.com/insights/single-source-of-truth-customer-feedback) first, because a pre-agreed threshold means nothing if two people are reading different numbers.


Evidence-based medicine has a name for the failure. The Cochrane Handbook describes["bias in selection of the reported result"](https://training.cochrane.org/handbook/current/chapter-13) , where authors pick a result to report from among several on the basis of its magnitude or direction. Their control is to fix the protocol first. Nosek and colleagues make the same case:[define the questions and the analysis plan before observing the outcomes](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1708274114) . Qualitative methodologists put it more bluntly: the interpretive framework "should be stipulated in advance and not decided post hoc after results are viewed."


In a planning meeting that's one question, asked at the start of a quarter rather than the end: what would we need to see to change this decision? A theme above a given share of feedback. A given movement in NPS points. A rising trend across two periods. Write it down before anyone has seen this quarter's comments.


The usual objection is that the feedback already exists, so nothing can really be pre-registered. The preregistration literature anticipates that and offers strategies for cases that fall short of the ideal, preexisting data among them. The point isn't purity. It's that the standard was set before anyone knew which way the evidence would fall. As Amazon's 2016 shareholder letter puts it,["You've worn me down" is an awful decision-making process](https://www.aboutamazon.com/md/news/company-news/2016-letter-to-shareholders) , and a well-chosen verbatim is a fast way to wear a room down.


## Rule 4: Let people test their own theory


The most durable counter isn't gatekeeping. It's making the set easy enough to query that a pet theory can be checked in a minute, usually by the person who holds it.


Thematic's Answers lets anyone[ask a question in plain English](https://getthematic.com/insights/ask-customer-feedback-questions-plain-english) and returns a narrative answer backed by data sources, verbatims and visuals, with a "Used data" view showing the datasets, filters and sentence volume behind it. The newer agentic version adds per-section citations you can follow into the analysis tools, and for low-sample questions returns the verbatims with their matched and total counts, which is the denominator problem solving itself. Filtered views can be shared as links, though the recipient needs a login and dataset permission, and PowerPoint exports carry the applied filters and sample size on the slide. Where the dispute is really about the dashboard,[executive-ready CX dashboards](https://getthematic.com/insights/cx-dashboards-that-earn-executive-trust) give each team a view of the same numbers.


Someone who has checked their own hunch and found it at 2% rarely brings it to the meeting. When they do, they bring the 2% with it.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Banning anecdotes.** Quotes are how findings become memorable. Constrain the format, don't remove the evidence.
- **Relying on the verbal caveat.** "This is only one customer" is the exact disclaimer the 1980 study showed doesn't work. Put the share on the slide.
- **Treating it as a sampling problem.** Whether your feedback is[representative of your customers](https://getthematic.com/insights/feedback-representative-not-loudest-customers) is a real and separate question. This one bites even when the dataset is sound.
- **Making it personal.** Selective quoting is usually inadvertent. A convention everyone follows is easier to adopt than a correction aimed at one person.
- **Setting the decision rule after the readout.** A threshold chosen once the numbers are visible isn't a threshold, it's a negotiation.


## The short answer


Change the format rather than policing the people. A percentage alone won't beat a vivid story, because the research says vividness is what moves a room. A second story, a threshold agreed before the data was seen, and a number everyone can trace will.
